\subsection{Structural Confound: Token Length and EOS Truncation}
\label{sec:length_confound}

A potential confound is that EOS truncation at the 256-token generation limit could create systematic length differences across depths, inflating AUC through a length shortcut rather than distributional signatures.
We quantify this concern across all model configurations (full per-depth statistics in Table~\ref{tab:token_length}).

Depth~0 (human text, truncated from C4) averages ${\sim}$191 tokens across all configurations, while depth~1+ (machine-generated) averages 195--256 tokens depending on model.
The length asymmetry thus runs \emph{opposite} to the confound direction: human texts are shorter, so any length-based shortcut would make 0v1 detection \emph{harder} (a classifier exploiting ``shorter$=$machine'' would fail), not easier.

Within machine-generated depths 1--5, token counts are remarkably stable.
For Qwen-rewrite, depths 1--5 average 252--254 tokens (range: 2 tokens); for Pythia, 214--218 tokens (range: 4 tokens); for Qwen-7B, 193--197 tokens (range: 4 tokens).
This stability means the critical $\Kempirical{=}2$ finding---based on 1v2 vs.\ 2v3 comparisons among machine-generated texts---cannot be driven by length differences, since depths 1 through 5 have effectively identical token counts within each model.

OLMo-1B provides the strongest control: it generates exactly 256 tokens at all depths 1--5 with $<$1\% EOS truncation (Table~\ref{tab:token_length}), completely eliminating length variation as a possible confound.
$\Kempirical{=}2$ holds for OLMo (1v2 $\auc = 0.615$, 2v3 $\auc = 0.550$; Table~\ref{tab:s8_cv_folds}), demonstrating that the depth boundary arises from distributional rather than length-based signals.

EOS truncation rates vary across models (Table~\ref{tab:token_length}): Qwen-rewrite and decoding ablations show mild truncation (7--16\% at depth~1+), Qwen-continuation moderate truncation (17--20\%), while Pythia (34--36\%) and Qwen-7B (45--47\%) exhibit higher rates.
Crucially, truncation rates are \emph{stable across depths 1--5 within each model}, so EOS effects do not create a depth-correlated length gradient that could confound pairwise discrimination.
The models with highest truncation (Pythia, Qwen-7B) still yield $\Kempirical{=}2$ with the same step-function AUC decay as low-truncation models, further ruling out length as a driver of the boundary.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\subsection{The One-Wash Laundering Effect}
\label{sec:why_kstar}
\label{sec:one_wash}

The shallowness of $\Kempirical = 2$ reflects the concentration of information loss: the 0v1 boundary is near-trivially separable ($\auc \geq 0.96$), 1v2 drops by ${\sim}$30\,pp, and 2v3 falls below $\theta$---the generation operator acts as a lossy channel with diminishing marginal information loss.
Consistency across four decoding strategies (Table~\ref{tab:s2_decoding}) reinforces that $\Kempirical$ is governed by the generation process rather than the sampling algorithm.
Even at the most marginal 1v2 condition (Qwen-continuation, CI lower bound exceeds $\theta$ by only 0.2\,pp), $\Kempirical = 2$ survives under self-scoring; on the 2v3 side, CI upper bounds confirm non-discrimination in 8/9 conditions, with the single borderline case (nucleus $p{=}0.9$, CI upper${} = 0.601$) consistent with measurement noise at near-threshold values.
Cross-scale validation at 7B (Section~\ref{sec:kstar_boundary}) extends this from 1.5B to 7B despite reduced 0v1 signal ($0.9638$ vs.\ $> 0.99$).

The practical consequence is a three-tier taxonomy: human-authored (depth~0), first-generation synthetic (depth~1), and deeper synthetic (depth~$\geq 2$).
A single generation pass suffices to render text statistically indistinguishable from multiply recycled content---a \emph{one-wash laundering} effect that limits depth-aware corpus curation to a binary boundary.
This connects to model collapse: Shumailov et al.~\cite{shumailov2024collapse} observed that tail-distribution degradation is most acute in the earliest generations; our prompt-chain results show an analogous per-text pattern.

Per-depth analysis provides the most direct evidence that this boundary is not methodological.
OBD achieves 96\% depth-0 recall but only 14--22\% for depths 2--4; frontier LLMs show 69--77\% depth-0 recall and 8--38\% for depths 2--4 (McNemar $p > 0.05$ vs.\ OBD; Table~\ref{tab:s3_llm_zeroshot}).
This convergence across fundamentally different approaches---supervised statistical classification and zero-shot frontier LLMs---provides converging evidence that the saturation reflects a data-intrinsic boundary rather than a method limitation.
Binary detector confidence corroborates: despite moderate Spearman correlations ($|\rho|$ up to 0.46), 6-class accuracy is at or below chance ($\leq 0.199$ vs.\ 0.167 baseline), and Qwen-rewrite exhibits a sign reversal ($\rho > 0$), disqualifying confidence as a reliable depth proxy.

\subsection{Why Graduated Filtering Fails}
\label{sec:negative_graduated}

Since 2v3 $\auc < \theta$ for all configurations, depth assignments for $d \geq 2$ approximate random labels; graduated weighting injects noise into importance weights, explaining the monotonic improvement with $\alpha$ as it converges toward binary thresholding (Appendix~\ref{sec:extended_limitations}).
DSIR fails for a different reason---bigram feature hashing captures domain shift but not depth-correlated distributional signatures.

\subsection{Representation Dependence of the Boundary}
\label{sec:repr_dependence}

$\Kempirical$ is representation-dependent: frozen Qwen embeddings yield $\Kempirical^{\text{neural}} = 3$, while Pythia and OLMo match the 15D boundary at $\Kempirical^{\text{neural}} = 2$ (Table~\ref{tab:neural_probe_crossmodel}).
The hierarchy $\Kempirical^{15\text{D}}{=}2 < \Kempirical^{\text{neural}} \in \{2,3\}$ reflects an interpretability--sensitivity tradeoff: learned representations recover additional depth signal sufficient to push $\Kempirical$ to 3 for one model (Qwen), but this gain is model-dependent---the 15D features trade one depth level of sensitivity for cross-model universality (9/9 conditions $\Kempirical{=}2$, 3/3 models identical), making them the preferred operational choice.

\label{sec:length_confound}

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\subsection{The One-Wash Laundering Effect}
\label{sec:why_kstar}
\label{sec:one_wash}

The shallowness of $\Kempirical = 2$ reflects the concentration of information loss: the 0v1 boundary is near-trivially separable ($\auc \geq 0.96$), 1v2 drops by ${\sim}$30\,pp, and 2v3 falls below $\theta$---the generation operator acts as a lossy channel with diminishing marginal information loss.
Consistency across four decoding strategies (Table~\ref{tab:s2_decoding}) reinforces that $\Kempirical$ is governed by the generation process rather than the sampling algorithm.
Even at the most marginal 1v2 condition (Qwen-continuation, CI lower bound exceeds $\theta$ by only 0.2\,pp), $\Kempirical = 2$ survives under self-scoring; on the 2v3 side, CI upper bounds confirm non-discrimination in 8/9 conditions, with the single borderline case (nucleus $p{=}0.9$, CI upper${} = 0.601$) consistent with measurement noise at near-threshold values.
Cross-scale validation at 7B (Section~\ref{sec:kstar_boundary}) extends this from 1.5B to 7B despite reduced 0v1 signal ($0.9638$ vs.\ $> 0.99$).

The practical consequence is a three-tier taxonomy: human-authored (depth~0), first-generation synthetic (depth~1), and deeper synthetic (depth~$\geq 2$).
A single generation pass suffices to render text statistically indistinguishable from multiply recycled content---a \emph{one-wash laundering} effect that limits depth-aware corpus curation to a binary boundary.
This connects to model collapse: Shumailov et al.~\cite{shumailov2024collapse} observed that tail-distribution degradation is most acute in the earliest generations; our prompt-chain results show an analogous per-text pattern.

Per-depth analysis provides the most direct evidence that this boundary is not methodological.
OBD achieves 96\% depth-0 recall but only 14--22\% for depths 2--4; frontier LLMs show 69--77\% depth-0 recall and 8--38\% for depths 2--4 (McNemar $p > 0.05$ vs.\ OBD; Table~\ref{tab:s3_llm_zeroshot}).
This convergence across fundamentally different approaches---supervised statistical classification and zero-shot frontier LLMs---provides converging evidence that the saturation reflects a data-intrinsic boundary rather than a method limitation.
Binary detector confidence corroborates: despite moderate Spearman correlations ($|\rho|$ up to 0.46), 6-class accuracy is at or below chance ($\leq 0.199$ vs.\ 0.167 baseline), and Qwen-rewrite exhibits a sign reversal ($\rho > 0$), disqualifying confidence as a reliable depth proxy.

\subsection{Why Graduated Filtering Fails}
\label{sec:negative_graduated}

Since 2v3 $\auc < \theta$ for all configurations, depth assignments for $d \geq 2$ approximate random labels; graduated weighting injects noise into importance weights, explaining the monotonic improvement with $\alpha$ as it converges toward binary thresholding (Appendix~\ref{sec:extended_limitations}).
DSIR fails for a different reason---bigram feature hashing captures domain shift but not depth-correlated distributional signatures.

\subsection{Representation Dependence of the Boundary}
\label{sec:repr_dependence}

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\subsection{The One-Wash Laundering Effect}
\label{sec:why_kstar}
\label{sec:one_wash}

The shallowness of $\Kempirical = 2$ reflects the concentration of information loss: the 0v1 boundary is near-trivially separable ($\auc \geq 0.96$), 1v2 drops by ${\sim}$30\,pp, and 2v3 falls below $\theta$---the generation operator acts as a lossy channel with diminishing marginal information loss.
Consistency across four decoding strategies (Table~\ref{tab:s2_decoding}) reinforces that $\Kempirical$ is governed by the generation process rather than the sampling algorithm.
Even at the most marginal 1v2 condition (Qwen-continuation, CI lower bound exceeds $\theta$ by only 0.2\,pp), $\Kempirical = 2$ survives under self-scoring; on the 2v3 side, CI upper bounds confirm non-discrimination in 8/9 conditions, with the single borderline case (nucleus $p{=}0.9$, CI upper${} = 0.601$) consistent with measurement noise at near-threshold values.
Cross-scale validation at 7B (Section~\ref{sec:kstar_boundary}) extends this from 1.5B to 7B despite reduced 0v1 signal ($0.9638$ vs.\ $> 0.99$).

The practical consequence is a three-tier taxonomy: human-authored (depth~0), first-generation synthetic (depth~1), and deeper synthetic (depth~$\geq 2$).
A single generation pass suffices to render text statistically indistinguishable from multiply recycled content---a \emph{one-wash laundering} effect that limits depth-aware corpus curation to a binary boundary.
This connects to model collapse: Shumailov et al.~\cite{shumailov2024collapse} observed that tail-distribution degradation is most acute in the earliest generations; our prompt-chain results show an analogous per-text pattern.

Per-depth analysis provides the most direct evidence that this boundary is not methodological.
OBD achieves 96\% depth-0 recall but only 14--22\% for depths 2--4; frontier LLMs show 69--77\% depth-0 recall and 8--38\% for depths 2--4 (McNemar $p > 0.05$ vs.\ OBD; Table~\ref{tab:s3_llm_zeroshot}).
This convergence across fundamentally different approaches---supervised statistical classification and zero-shot frontier LLMs---provides converging evidence that the saturation reflects a data-intrinsic boundary rather than a method limitation.
Binary detector confidence corroborates: despite moderate Spearman correlations ($|\rho|$ up to 0.46), 6-class accuracy is at or below chance ($\leq 0.199$ vs.\ 0.167 baseline), and Qwen-rewrite exhibits a sign reversal ($\rho > 0$), disqualifying confidence as a reliable depth proxy.

\subsection{Why Graduated Filtering Fails}
\label{sec:negative_graduated}

Since 2v3 $\auc < \theta$ for all configurations, depth assignments for $d \geq 2$ approximate random labels; graduated weighting injects noise into importance weights, explaining the monotonic improvement with $\alpha$ as it converges toward binary thresholding (Appendix~\ref{sec:extended_limitations}).
DSIR fails for a different reason---bigram feature hashing captures domain shift but not depth-correlated distributional signatures.

\subsection{Representation Dependence of the Boundary}
\label{sec:repr_dependence}

$\Kempirical$ is representation-dependent: frozen Qwen embeddings yield $\Kempirical^{\text{neural}} = 3$, while Pythia and OLMo match the 15D boundary at $\Kempirical^{\text{neural}} = 2$ (Table~\ref{tab:neural_probe_crossmodel}).
The hierarchy $\Kempirical^{15\text{D}}{=}2 < \Kempirical^{\text{neural}} \in \{2,3\}$ reflects an interpretability--sensitivity tradeoff: learned representations recover additional depth signal sufficient to push $\Kempirical$ to 3 for one model (Qwen), but this gain is model-dependent---the 15D features trade one depth level of sensitivity for cross-model universality (9/9 conditions $\Kempirical{=}2$, 3/3 models identical), making them the preferred operational choice.
Cross-scorer validation reinforces this: alternative scorers preserve feature rankings ($\rho > 0.90$) but reduce the marginal Qwen-continuation boundary from $\Kempirical = 2$ to 1, while rewrite-mode $\Kempirical = 2$ is preserved---$\Kempirical$ is governed by the generation operator rather than the scoring model.

\subsection{Structural Confound: Token Length and EOS Truncation}
\label{sec:length_confound}

A potential confound is that EOS truncation at the 256-token generation limit could create systematic length differences across depths, inflating AUC through a length shortcut rather than distributional signatures.
We quantify this concern across all model configurations (full per-depth statistics in Table~\ref{tab:token_length}).

Depth~0 (human text, truncated from C4) averages ${\sim}$191 tokens across all configurations, while depth~1+ (machine-generated) averages 193--256 tokens depending on model.
The length asymmetry thus runs \emph{opposite} to the confound direction: human texts are shorter, so any length-based shortcut would make 0v1 detection \emph{harder} (a classifier exploiting ``shorter$=$machine'' would fail), not easier.

In continuation mode, the generation prompt (first half of the predecessor text) is discarded; only the newly generated tokens are retained as the depth-$k$ text.
Consequently, all texts at depths $\geq 1$ consist entirely of machine-generated content, and the 1v2 boundary compares texts that differ only in their conditioning context (human-authored vs.\ machine-generated prompt), not in their structural composition.

Within machine-generated depths 1--5, token counts are remarkably stable.
For Qwen-rewrite, depths 1--5 average 252--254 tokens (range: 2 tokens); for Pythia, 214--218 tokens (range: 4 tokens); for Qwen-7B, 193--197 tokens (range: 4 tokens).
This stability means the critical $\Kempirical{=}2$ finding---based on 1v2 vs.\ 2v3 comparisons among machine-generated texts---cannot be driven by length differences, since depths 1 through 5 have effectively identical token counts within each model.

OLMo-1B provides the strongest control: it generates exactly 256 tokens at all depths 1--5 with $<$1\% EOS truncation (Table~\ref{tab:token_length}), completely eliminating length variation as a possible confound.
$\Kempirical{=}2$ holds for OLMo (1v2 $\auc = 0.615$, 2v3 $\auc = 0.550$; Table~\ref{tab:s8_cv_folds}), demonstrating that the depth boundary arises from distributional rather than length-based signals.

EOS truncation rates vary across models (Table~\ref{tab:token_length}): Qwen-rewrite and decoding ablations show mild truncation (7--16\% at depth~1+), Qwen-continuation moderate truncation (17--20\%), while Pythia (34--36\%) and Qwen-7B (45--47\%) exhibit higher rates.
Crucially, truncation rates are \emph{stable across depths 1--5 within each model}, so EOS effects do not create a depth-correlated length gradient that could confound pairwise discrimination.
The models with highest truncation (Pythia, Qwen-7B) still yield $\Kempirical{=}2$ with the same step-function AUC decay as low-truncation models, further ruling out length as a driver of the boundary.

lines: The hierarchy $\Kempirical^{15\text{D}}{=}2 < \Kempirical^{\text{neural}} \in \{2,3\}$ reflects an interpretability--sensitivity tradeoff: learned representations recover additional depth signal sufficient to push $\Kempirical$ to 3 for one model (Qwen), but this gain is model-dependent---the 15D features trade one depth level of sensitivity for cross-model universality (9/9 conditions $\Kempirical{=}2$, 3/3 models identical), making them the preferred operational choice.

Cross-scorer validation reinforces this: alternative scorers preserve feature rankings ($\rho > 0.90$) but reduce the marginal Qwen-continuation boundary from $\Kempirical = 2$ to 1, while rewrite-mode $\Kempirical = 2$ is preserved---$\Kempirical$ is governed by the generation operator rather than the scoring model.
-\subsection{Structural Confound: Token Length}
+\paragraph{Structural confound.}
\label{sec:length_confound}

-In continuation mode, the generation prompt is discarded; only the newly generated tokens are retained as the depth-$k$ text, so all texts at depths $\geq 1$ consist entirely of machine-generated content and the 1v2 boundary compares texts differing only in conditioning context (human-authored vs.\ machine-generated prompt), not structural composition.
-Depth~0 averages ${\sim}$191 tokens while depth~1+ averages 193--256 tokens depending on model---a length asymmetry that makes 0v1 detection \emph{more conservative}, not inflated.

-Within depths 1--5, token counts are stable (within-model range $\leq$ 6 tokens) and EOS truncation rates are depth-invariant, so the $\Kempirical{=}2$ boundary cannot be driven by length differences; OLMo-1B ($<$1\% truncation, identical 256 tokens at all depths) provides the strongest control and still yields $\Kempirical{=}2$ (full statistics in Table~\ref{tab:token_length}, Appendix~\ref{sec:extended_limitations}).

lines: $\Kempirical$ is representation-dependent: frozen Qwen embeddings yield $\Kempirical^{\text{neural}} = 3$, while Pythia and OLMo match the 15D boundary at $\Kempirical^{\text{neural}} = 2$ (Table~\ref{tab:neural_probe_crossmodel}).

The hierarchy $\Kempirical^{15\text{D}}{=}2 < \Kempirical^{\text{neural}} \in \{2,3\}$ reflects an interpretability--sensitivity tradeoff: learned representations recover additional depth signal sufficient to push $\Kempirical$ to 3 for one model (Qwen), but this gain is model-dependent---the 15D features trade one depth level of sensitivity for cross-model universality (9/9 conditions $\Kempirical{=}2$, 3/3 models identical), making them the preferred operational choice.

Cross-scorer validation reinforces this: alternative scorers preserve feature rankings ($\rho > 0.90$) but reduce the marginal Qwen-continuation boundary from $\Kempirical = 2$ to 1, while rewrite-mode $\Kempirical = 2$ is preserved---$\Kempirical$ is governed by the generation operator rather than the scoring model.
-\paragraph{Structural confound.}

+A potential length confound is also ruled out: in continuation mode the generation prompt is discarded so all depths $\geq 1$ are purely machine-generated, token counts are stable within depths 1--5 ($\leq$ 6-token range), and the length asymmetry (depth~0 ${\sim}$191 vs.\ depth~1+ 193--256 tokens) makes 0v1 detection more conservative, not inflated (Appendix~\ref{sec:extended_limitations}).

1	\section{Experiments}
2	\label{sec:experiments}
3	
4	We evaluate generational depth estimation on five model configurations:
5	Pythia-1.4B and OLMo-1B in continuation mode, Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct in both rewrite and continuation modes, and Qwen2.5-7B in continuation mode (cross-scale scoring with Qwen2.5-1.5B).
6	All experiments use the OBD-LightGBM classifier with the 15-dimensional feature set (Section~\ref{sec:method}), with 5{,}000 texts per depth level (generations 0--5).
7	
8	%% ====================================================================
9	\subsection{$\Kempirical = 2$ Across All Configurations}
10	\label{sec:kstar_boundary}
11	
12	\begin{table*}[t]
13	\centering
14	\small
15	\caption{Pairwise $\auc$ for adjacent depth pairs with bootstrap 95\% CIs and permutation $p$-values for boundary rows.

38	\caption{Pairwise $\auc$ decay across depth pairs for model-mode configurations (solid) and decoding strategies (dashed). The horizontal dashed line marks $\theta = 0.60$.}
39	\label{fig:auc_decay}
40	\end{figure}
41	
42	Table~\ref{tab:kstar_ci} and Figure~\ref{fig:auc_decay} show a consistent pattern: 0v1 discrimination is near-perfect ($\auc \geq 0.96$), followed by a sharp drop at 1v2 ($\auc$: 0.6112--0.6955), with 2v3 falling below $\theta$ (0.5492--0.5893) and deeper pairs converging toward chance.
43	All five 1v2 point estimates exceed $\theta$, confirmed by bootstrap CIs (most marginal lower bound: Qwen-1.5B-continuation at 0.602); all five 2v3 point estimates and CI upper bounds fall below $\theta$ (permutation $p < 0.001$ for all boundary comparisons).
44	This establishes $\Kempirical = 2$ as consistent across all 9 tested conditions (5 independent model-mode configurations and 4 decoding-strategy ablation variants on the Qwen-rewrite configuration; Table~\ref{tab:s2_decoding}).
45	Under cross-model scoring, Qwen-continuation $\Kempirical$ drops to 1 (Section~\ref{sec:transfer}), indicating a model-specific component in the most marginal 1v2 boundary signal.
46	The sharp step-function pattern reflects the concentration of information loss: human text exhibits heavy-tailed, bursty surprisal patterns that are substantially altered by even a single autoregressive pass.
47	Subsequent generations operate on already-smoothed distributions, yielding progressively smaller marginal changes that fall below detectability within two steps.
48	
49	The 1v2 $\auc$ varies across models: Qwen-rewrite (0.6955) $>$ Pythia (0.6539) $>$ OLMo (0.6145) $\approx$ Qwen-continuation (0.6112).
50	The spread due to generation mode within a single model ($\Delta = 8.4$\,pp) exceeds the spread across models in the same mode ($\Delta = 3.9$\,pp), suggesting that generation mode appears to have a larger effect than model architecture, though formal interaction testing is beyond our current scope.
51	
52	\paragraph{Cross-scale validation.}
53	Qwen2.5-7B in continuation mode (scored by Qwen2.5-1.5B) confirms $\Kempirical = 2$: 1v2 $\auc = 0.6168$ $[0.608,\,0.626]$ (CI lower bound $> \theta$), 2v3 $\auc = 0.5492$ $[0.539,\,0.559]$ (Table~\ref{tab:kstar_ci}).
54	The 0v1 $\auc$ drops to 0.9638 (${\sim}$3\,pp below ${\leq}$1.5B models), consistent with larger models generating more human-like text; yet the $\Kempirical$ boundary remains unchanged, extending the invariance from 1.5B to 7B.

The dashed line marks the operational threshold $\theta{=}0.60$ used throughout, where all configurations yield $\Kempirical{=}2$. Qwen-rewrite yields the highest $\Kempirical$ at all $\theta$; at $\theta{=}0.70$, $\Kempirical{=}1$ universally.}
60	\label{fig:kstar_theta}
61	\end{figure}

6	\label{sec:one_wash}

8	The shallowness of $\Kempirical = 2$ reflects the concentration of information loss: the 0v1 boundary is near-trivially separable ($\auc \geq 0.96$), 1v2 drops by ${\sim}$30\,pp, and 2v3 falls below $\theta$---the generation operator acts as a lossy channel with diminishing marginal information loss.

12	
13	The practical consequence is a three-tier taxonomy: human-authored (depth~0), first-generation synthetic (depth~1), and deeper synthetic (depth~$\geq 2$).
14	A single generation pass suffices to render text statistically indistinguishable from multiply recycled content---a \emph{one-wash laundering} effect that limits depth-aware corpus curation to a binary boundary.
15	This connects to model collapse: Shumailov et al.~\cite{shumailov2024collapse} observed that tail-distribution degradation is most acute in the earliest generations; our prompt-chain results show an analogous per-text pattern.
16	
17	Per-depth analysis provides the most direct evidence that this boundary is not methodological.
18	OBD achieves 96\% depth-0 recall but only 14--22\% for depths 2--4; frontier LLMs show 69--77\% depth-0 recall and 8--38\% for depths 2--4 (McNemar $p > 0.05$ vs.\ OBD; Table~\ref{tab:s3_llm_zeroshot}).

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

We presented the first systematic measurement of the generational depth discrimination boundary $\Kempirical$ for recursive synthetic text.
Two primary findings emerge:
(a)~$\Kempirical = 2$ at $\theta{=}0.60$ (Cohen's $h{\approx}0.20$), consistent across all tested configurations from 1B to 7B under self-scoring ($p \leq 0.002$; most marginal: 0.2\,pp above $\theta$), implying a one-wash laundering effect.
Convergent failure of both supervised classifiers and frontier LLMs at depths $\geq 2$ (McNemar $p > 0.05$) provides converging evidence consistent with this reflecting a data-intrinsic boundary rather than a method limitation.
Generation mode appears to have a larger effect than model architecture ($\Delta = 8.4$\,pp), but rewrite-mode advantages are non-transferable (61--63\% vs.\ 80--92\%).
(b)~Model-free statistical features enable 80--92\% cross-model transfer retention among continuation-mode generators with scorer-invariant feature ordering ($\rho > 0.90$), with surprisal-variance features dominating across model families ($\rho \geq 0.85$); cross-scorer validation confirms that $\Kempirical$ is governed by the generation process rather than the scoring model, enabling depth estimation for text from unknown generators without retraining.
As a downstream validation, $\Kempirical = 2$ correctly predicts the optimal curation granularity: binary filtering minimizes degradation most effectively; finer ordinal structure and depth-agnostic methods (DSIR) provide no benefit.

Future work includes scaling beyond 7B, extending to naturalistic multi-domain corpora, and developing model-agnostic neural probes.
Our prompt-chain protocol isolates generation-level information loss in a controlled setting; establishing the retrain-chain $\Kstar$ relationship, where training dynamics introduce additional degradation, is a natural next step.
The 100\% synthetic filtering experiment characterizes an upper bound; mixed-corpus dose-response and base-vs.-instruct comparisons (partially controlled by our continuation-mode analysis) remain open.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Web-scale text corpora are increasingly contaminated by synthetic content that has itself been generated from earlier synthetic content.
Estimates suggest that a substantial fraction of online text is machine-generated~\cite{sun2025aigt, spennemann2025quantifying}, and this share continues to rise.
When models train on the outputs of earlier models, the resulting multi-generational synthetic text degrades with each iteration: tail modes vanish, lexical diversity contracts, and surprisal distributions flatten~\cite{shumailov2024collapse, dohmatob2024model}.
This degradation arises in both \emph{retrain-chains} (iteratively training on model outputs) and \emph{prompt-chains} (recursively generating from previous outputs without retraining); we study the latter, which isolates generation-level information loss from training dynamics (Appendix~\ref{sec:extended_limitations}).
Yet the dominant paradigm treats all machine-generated text identically, discarding the generational depth dimension.

The gap cuts across three communities.
Binary detection methods~\cite{basani2026diveye, zhang2024minkpp} produce no depth estimate, and their confidence scores fail to discriminate beyond the binary boundary (Section~\ref{sec:binary_confidence}).
Data contamination detection via membership inference~\cite{zawalski2026codec} addresses a different question (whether specific texts appeared in training data) and likewise provides no depth signal.
The model collapse literature~\cite{shumailov2024collapse, alemohammad2024selfconsuming, schaeffer2025position} characterizes recursive degradation at the macro level but provides no per-text depth estimation tool.
Data selection methods~\cite{xie2023dsir, tirumala2023d4, drayson2025} ignore recursive depth.
No existing method estimates how many rounds of recursive generation a text has undergone, nor quantifies the boundary beyond which such estimation becomes infeasible.

The Data Processing Inequality guarantees that information degrades monotonically across generations, motivating a finite discrimination boundary $\Kstar$.
We empirically measure $\Kempirical$---the maximum depth at which a classifier reliably distinguishes adjacent generations---using 15 statistical features and an Ordinal Binary Decomposition (OBD) LightGBM classifier.
We operationalize $\Kempirical$ as the deepest $k \geq 1$ where the bootstrap 95\% CI for pairwise $\auc_{k-1,k}$ exceeds $\theta = 0.60$.

Our contributions center on two empirical findings:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*),nosep]
  \item \textbf{$\Kempirical = 2$ at $\theta{=}0.60$} (Cohen's $h{\approx}0.20$) across 5 model configurations (1B--7B) and 4 decoding strategies, with all 1v2 CI lower bounds exceeding $\theta$ and all 2v3 CI upper bounds below $\theta$ ($p \leq 0.002$; Section~\ref{sec:kstar_boundary}).
  Generation mode appears to have a larger effect than model architecture ($+$8.4\,pp rewrite vs.\ continuation within Qwen; $3.9$\,pp spread across continuation-mode models), though formal interaction testing is beyond our current scope.
  This is independently corroborated: both supervised OBD and zero-shot frontier LLMs fail comparably at depths $\geq 2$ (McNemar $p > 0.05$), providing converging evidence consistent with $\Kempirical{=}2$ reflecting a data-intrinsic boundary (Section~\ref{sec:why_kstar}).
  \item \textbf{Model-free cross-model transfer}: 15 statistical features enable 80--92\% accuracy retention across continuation-mode generators with scorer-invariant feature ordering ($\rho > 0.90$; Section~\ref{sec:transfer}), with surprisal-variance features dominating ($\rho \geq 0.85$).
  Cross-scorer validation confirms that $\Kempirical$ is governed by the generation process rather than the scoring model.
\end{enumerate}

\noindent As a downstream validation, $\Kempirical = 2$ correctly predicts the strategy ordering in data filtering: binary curation at the $\Kempirical$ boundary minimizes degradation most effectively (MMLU $0.5941$ vs.\ base $0.6018$), while graduated ($0.5892$) and surprisal-based ($0.5894$) strategies provide no additional benefit (Section~\ref{sec:filtering}).

lines: \section{Experiments}
\label{sec:experiments}
-We evaluate generational depth estimation on five model configurations:
-Pythia-1.4B and OLMo-1B in continuation mode, Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct in both rewrite and continuation modes, and Qwen2.5-7B in continuation mode (cross-scale scoring with Qwen2.5-1.5B).
+We evaluate generational depth estimation on six model configurations:

+Pythia-1.4B and OLMo-1B in continuation mode, Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct in both rewrite and continuation modes, Qwen2.5-1.5B (base) in continuation mode, and Qwen2.5-7B in continuation mode (cross-scale scoring with Qwen2.5-1.5B).
All experiments use the OBD-LightGBM classifier with the 15-dimensional feature set (Section~\ref{sec:method}), with 5{,}000 texts per depth level (generations 0--5).
